thread.title: Bryan Trottier honored with Canadian stamp recognizing Indigenous sports leaders
thread.title_full: Bryan Trottier honored with Canadian stamp recognizing Indigenous sports leaders

author: y. r. walker
title: Bryan Trottier honored with Canadian stamp recognizing Indigenous sports leaders
text:
Bryan Trottier said on June 17 that receiving his own Canadian postage stamp is the highest honor he could receive from his country. The stamp is part of a new issue by Canada Post celebrating Canadian Indigenous leaders and advocates in sports.
Trottier, who grew up in Val Marie, Saskatchewan, said he dreamed of becoming a National Hockey League player and winning the Stanley Cup but never imagined being featured on a postage stamp. “It’s probably the highest honor I can get from my country, Canada,” Trottier said. “The fact that it recognizes my Indigenous roots and the country of my birth and the fun stuff that’s happened to me over the course of my life, you can’t dream about that.”
Canada Post unveiled three stamps at Calgary Public Library — Central honoring Trottier; Edward Lennie, an advocate for Arctic sports; and Chief Wilton Littlechild, a former member of Parliament and athlete who promoted Indigenous sports. The issue is part of an ongoing series launched in 2022 highlighting contributions from First Nations, Inuit, and Metis leaders dedicated to preserving culture and improving quality of life for Indigenous peoples in Canada.
“This is one of the highest honors, very special because it recognizes something beyond just my abilities and skills in hockey,” Trottier said. He added, “My grandparents, my father, my uncles, all the family went through the discrimination aspects of the times… To be able to do the stuff I was able to do…and have it recognized on a postage stamp in Canada, it’s hard to put into words the honor that comes with that.”
The Trottier stamp features him as a New York Islanders player hoisting the Stanley Cup against a prairie landscape backdrop. Designed by Tétro with photography by Bruce Bennett/Getty Images and background by Branimir Gjetvaj, Trottier described its appearance as “regal.” A second-round pick by New York in 1974, he won four consecutive Stanley Cups with them (1980–1983), two more with Pittsburgh Penguins (1991–1992), another as assistant coach for Colorado Avalanche (2001), several NHL awards including Calder Trophy (1976) and Hart Trophy (1979), accumulated 1,425 points over his career before being inducted into Hockey Hall of Fame in 1997.
Trottier identifies as Cree, Metis, Chippewa and Irish heritage. He co-founded Aboriginal Alumni Hockey Team visiting communities across Canada mentoring youth: “I think for me it’s just about inspiring the next generation… Whether you’re Metis, Chippewa or Algonquin… You can achieve.”
The commemorative booklet includes six Permanent stamps plus three Official First Day Covers depicting scenes from his career along with biographical information available online at canadapost.ca or selected postal outlets starting June 19.
